title: School Year Shut Down: Getting Our Souls Ready for Summer
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Opening his "School Year Shut Down" series, Dave describes a reflective walk to work in which he thought about the students he taught, colleagues retiring, and what's next for him professionally. He commits to a summer series of brief exercises meant to help teachers shut down their school years intentionally, arguing that beginnings and endings matter not just for students but for teachers' own souls, and closes with a suggested weekend walking-reflection exercise.
points: Frames "shutting down" a school year as an intentional practice worth ritualizing, not just something that happens to teachers when the calendar runs out.

Models reflection on three specific prompts during a walk — students taught that year, colleagues retiring or leaving the profession, and what feels like "next" professionally — offering a template readers can reuse.

States plainly that beginnings and endings in teaching matter "not just because of how they impact our students" but because they matter for teachers themselves, reframing end-of-year rituals as self-care rather than just classroom closure.
Announces the piece as the first in a multi-part series, setting up the "School Year Shut Down" framework used across several other pieces archived from this same period.
quotes: On the walk, I spent some time reflecting on the school year that's drawing to a close. On the students I've gotten to teach, whose faces I've gotten to know; on the countless colleagues I admire who won't be teaching next year, heading into earlier-than-expected retirements.

Teaching and writing, helping schools and teams, learning and sharing: these aren't going anywhere for me. Whether the coming year's labors help 1 or 100 students, help 1 or 1,000 colleagues — I intend to do it.
But that doesn't mean I intend to ignore my soul's need for rest this summer.
Beginnings and endings are important in this work — but not just because of how they impact our students. They're important for us, too.
The walk won't resolve all the hard and difficult and confusing that these questions may bring; but amidst all that muck, I promise there's good.
